evidence: The brief and all three notes read as one person at a small firm talking about their own practice, with reasons attached to requirements, and they keep that voice throughout. instruction.md:1 opens with a real pain point: 'our clients keep emailing documents to whoever answered last'. instruction.md:3 uses plain, slightly informal phrasing: 'from any corner of the app', 'so old chat doesn't pile up', 'what has gone must stay gone'. instruction.md:9 is a casual request: 'please try it the way we'll use it ... and make sure nothing breaks'. The notes keep the same first-person 'we/our' voice and give motivations instead of acceptance bullets. conversations.md:5 says 'Our clients ask several things at once, so answers have to stay with their question'; :9 says 'People fix typos and figures'; :13 says 'Clients paste all sorts into chat'; :29 says 'Our internet in court is patchy.'; :31 says 'That must not disturb what I'm doing'. walls-and-retention.md:17 says 'because a leak is a professional-conduct problem for us'; :19 says 'Conflicts come up mid-matter'. integration.md:5 says 'we won't run an app that has them'; :7 says 'which is why we care that the order stays consistent'. Sentence length varies. There are short lines such as walls-and-retention.md:3 'Everyone signs in with `password123`.', :15 'Dev Anand is walled from M-12 today.' and conversations.md:29 'Our internet in court is patchy.', alongside longer explanatory sentences. I found contractions in every file: doesn't, we'll, can't, mustn't, don't, I'm, I've, isn't, won't, aren't. A grep for marketing or LLM tells (seamless|robust|delve|ensure|leverage|comprehensive|intuitive|user-friendly|streamlin|utiliz|crucial|furthermore|moreover|additionally|em dash|shall) found no matches. There are no bulleted or numbered acceptance lists. The only table is the account roster in walls-and-retention.md:5-11, which is ordinary reference data. The voice does not change between instruction.md and the notes. The notes' H1 titles also stay in that voice: 'How we talk in a matter' and 'How we run it'. Minor observations, not defects: (a) Some note paragraphs list items densely, which tilts toward precise rather than casual: walls-and-retention.md:17 lists every leak route, :35 describes the transcript contents, and conversations.md:13 lists every place a message appears. Each list is still written as running prose with a reason attached, so it is not robotic bullet parallelism. Whether the notes read as a checklist belongs to row 1 and other rows. (b) conversations.md:25 and :31 switch from 'we' to 'I' ('When I open a matter', 'what I'm doing'). That is a natural shift for one staff member writing for the firm, not a change of register. Two adversarial cases are relevant to this row. First, could LLM-polished prose pass this review? I checked for its hallmarks (uniform cadence, gloss vocabulary, parallel bullets, hedged transitions) and found none. Second, would a natural brief fail this row? No: the text matches the row's 'casual/terse is good' standard. This row judges the text only. No runtime, Oracle, model or portal measurement is involved or claimed. The verdict is a source judgement on the frozen bytes listed above, and a hosted reviewer's subjective reading could still differ.
